lesson.title: Adding It All Up: The Arithmetic Mean
lesson.summary: The mean is the arithmetic average of a quantitative variable's values, calculated by summing every observation and dividing by the count, and it is the most commonly used but most outlier-sensitive measure of center.
lesson.body:
The mean, often just called the average in everyday language, is the most familiar measure of the center of a distribution. It is calculated by adding up every value in a data set and dividing that total by the number of values, formally written as mean equals the sum of all observations divided by n, the sample size. Because this calculation requires adding actual numeric values together, the mean only makes sense for a quantitative variable, a variable measured on a numeric scale like test scores, heights, or prices, connecting directly to that concept: you cannot meaningfully average a categorical variable like favorite color or blood type.

Consider seven quiz scores: 85, 90, 78, 92, 88, 95, and 70. Adding them together: 85 + 90 = 175, plus 78 is 253, plus 92 is 345, plus 88 is 433, plus 95 is 528, plus 70 is 598. Dividing the total, 598, by the count, 7, gives 598 divided by 7, which is approximately 85.43. This single number, 85.43, is meant to represent a "typical" score across all seven students, even though no individual student actually scored exactly that.

The mean's greatest strength is also its greatest weakness: it uses every single value in the data set in its calculation, which makes it sensitive to the exact size of every observation, including extreme ones. This is precisely why, in the right-skewed home price example earlier in this unit, a single 900-thousand-dollar home pulled the mean up to 317.5 while the median stayed near 205, and why, in the center-of-distribution example with six people's ages, the one 60-year-old pulled the mean up to about 29.67 even though the other five people were all in their early twenties. Whenever a distribution has a long tail or contains an outlier, the mean gets dragged in the direction of that tail or outlier, sometimes to the point where it no longer represents a realistic typical value at all.

Despite this sensitivity, the mean remains the single most widely used measure of center in statistics, largely because it has convenient mathematical properties that later, more advanced topics rely on, including its role in calculating variance and standard deviation, and its predictable behavior when combining or scaling data. For distributions that are roughly symmetric with no substantial outliers, the mean is an excellent, efficient summary of center, since it uses all the available information rather than just a middle value or a most-frequent value.

The rule of thumb worth remembering going forward is this: report the mean when a distribution is roughly symmetric, but be cautious about relying on it, or pair it with the median, whenever a distribution is skewed or contains outliers, since those are exactly the situations where the mean and the more resistant median, covered next, are most likely to disagree.
